title: Place and Worth Chart
context: Grade 4, and this topic carries two words that look like one word. The place of a digit is where it sits, and it is a name. The place value of a digit is what it is worth sitting there, and it is an amount. The chapter's own worked example asks for place values and then answers every line with the word place, so a class reading it cold will learn the two as one and answer a place value question with the word tenths, which names the column again and never says how much.

writeup.why: Carry your place chart past the ones, and then say two different things about one digit: where it sits, and how much it is worth there.
writeup.look: A ruled chart with a heading over every column, a dot column between the ones and the tenths, two answer slots under it and a rebuild bar along the foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Place and Worth Chart' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the digits settled against the digits the chart is holding, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each digit is given both a name and an amount and the second fixed at the width of the number. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The chart fills the top of the working area, its headings row 48 tall at 64,206 and its cells 96 tall at 64,254. Seven digit columns stand 130 wide and one narrow column 70 wide holds the dot, in this order from the left: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones, the dot column, tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Every column carries a named heading written above it, outside the chart, and holds one digit and one only; a column already holding a digit refuses a second and springs it back with nothing marked. Grow the chart extends the ruled ground past the ones through the dot column and names each new column as it appears, left to right, so the three decimal places arrive in the order they are made. Count from the point runs rightwards from the dot column, lighting and naming one column at a time, and it always begins at the dot and never at either end of the number. The two answer slots stand under the chart, the place slot 360 by 88 at 64,386 and the worth slot 360 by 88 at 460,386, each with its heading drawn above it. Neither will take the other's answer: a column name dropped into the worth slot springs back with the column it names lit and the slot left empty, and an amount dropped into the place slot springs back the same way, with nothing marked and nothing cleared either time. The whole number bay stands at 860,386, 240 by 180, and asks how many tens, hundreds or thousands sit inside a long whole number, which is this same chart read the other way along. The rebuild bar runs at 64,510, 1080 by 130: every worth that has been given is carried down into it and stands in a visible row with its plus signs drawn between, the row is added, and the total is stood beside a copy of the number the chart started from, where the two are read digit for digit. The card lane runs along the foot, 1080 by 80 at 64,650, handing out digit cards and a single point card for holders to arrange, and refusing an arrangement with the point standing first or last by naming the rule it broke and nothing else. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a digit or an amount is asked for, with a fraction key beside them that draws a bar and opens a box above and a box below, and above the keys a name tray carrying the eight column headings, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths with the dot beside them, whose keys will only go into the slot headed place. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception. A part or a column standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The dot is given a column of its own on this chart and is never tucked into the ones column or drawn hanging off the edge of a digit. It is the one column that holds no digit, it is the column every count of places starts from, and a chart drawn without it is a chart where the counting has nowhere to begin.
writeup.finish: The card shows the chart the child filled, each digit under its named column, and the rebuild bar standing under it with its total.

phases.win: the dot column and the three decimal columns settle, each one named over its head
phases.does: grows the chart past the ones and names each new column as it appears
phases.goal: the chart the child already knows grows rightwards past the ones, through a dot
phases.says: Your chart stops at the ones. What could come after it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: draw your own chart from the thousands to the thousandths, headings first, and mark the dot its own column.
phases.feels: the chart does not stop, it carries on getting smaller past the ones
phases.hands: Draw the chart by hand across a whole page, headings first and a narrow column kept for the dot between the ones and whatever comes after it. Do not write a single digit until every heading is written. Ask what could come after the ones column and why the chart is allowed to carry on at all, and let the class answer from the strip and the grid they cut earlier rather than from memory.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which column is the last one you already knew? Second rung, the phase's: is the next piece along bigger or smaller than a whole one? Third rung: the chart is cut to ones, dot and tenths and the child names all three. The name tray stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: on the left of the chart the columns grow as the eye travels left, and nothing announces that the direction turns round at the dot.
wrong.move: reads the columns after the point leftwards, the way the whole number columns are read, so tenths ends up at the far right.
wrong.screen: the chart is grown again from the ones outwards with each new column named as it appears and a piece of the right size drawn under it, the amber tenth first, the rose hundredth next and the sky blue thousandth last, so the pieces get smaller as the columns travel right. The child's headings stay exactly where they were placed, and the two readings of the chart stand one above the other.

wrong.why: the dot is small and it sits right beside the ones digit, so it looks like a mark on that digit rather than a thing with a place of its own.
wrong.move: puts the dot inside the ones column instead of giving it a column of its own.
wrong.screen: the chart redraws with the narrow dot column ruled between the ones and the tenths and the dot standing in it, and count from the point is run twice: once from the child's chart, where the count has to start inside a column that is already holding a digit, and once from the chart with the dot column, where it starts on empty ground. Both charts are left standing.

phases.screen: the familiar chart ending at the ones with empty ground to its right
phases.soWhat: The place value chart runs on to the right of the ones place, past a dot, as tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
phases.concept: The chart carries on past the point

phases.win: the counted columns light one at a time and the chosen column takes its name
phases.does: counts rightwards from the dot and names the column a chosen digit sits in
phases.goal: position alone decides the place, whatever the digit happens to be
phases.says: Count along from the dot. Where does this one sit?
phases.check: In a number of your own with three digits after the point, say which place the last one sits in and how you found it.
phases.feels: the column decides, and the digit standing in it has no say in the matter
phases.hands: Write a number with three digits after the point on the board and ask for the place of one digit at a time, in no particular order, with the class counting aloud from the dot each time rather than answering from the shape of the number. Then change one digit for a much bigger one, leave it where it is, and ask whether its place has changed.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: where is the dot in this number? Second rung, the phase's: how many columns along from it is this digit? Third rung: the chart is cut to the dot and two columns after it and the child names both. The name tray stays open.

wrong.why: size and importance have gone together in every number met so far, and a big digit looks as though it ought to be worth more than a small one beside it.
wrong.move: gives the larger digit the larger place, so an eight is put ahead of a four whatever order they stand in.
wrong.screen: count from the point runs along the columns one at a time with each heading lighting as it is passed, and the digits are read out in the order they are standing rather than by size. The child's answer stays in the slot, the two digits are then swapped over in the chart with their places read again, and both readings are left on the stage.

wrong.why: numbers are read from the left, and on a number with one digit in front of the point the two counts happen to land on the same column, which is enough for the habit to survive unnoticed.
wrong.move: counts the decimal places from the left hand end of the number instead of from the point.
wrong.screen: the counting runs twice with both runs left drawn and numbered over the columns: once from the left hand end of the number, which is still inside the whole number part when it stops, and once from the dot outwards. A second number with three digits in front of the point is then dropped into the chart, where the two counts plainly part, and the child's count stays written where it was made.

phases.screen: a number dropped into the chart with its columns still unnamed
phases.soWhat: Position alone decides a digit's place, and the places are counted from the point outwards.

phases.win: both slots fill with answers of the right kind and the lit column holds the two together
phases.does: fills the place slot with a name and the worth slot with an amount
phases.goal: the place is a name and the place value is an amount
phases.says: Where does it sit? Now say how much it is worth sitting there.
phases.check: Take the first digit after the point in a number of your own. Give its place, and then give its place value.
phases.feels: two questions about one digit, and the answers are different kinds of thing
phases.hands: Ask for the place first and the worth second, in that order, every single time, and write the two answers in two separate columns on the board so they never run together. Take one digit and ask both questions about it, then ask the class which of the two answers is a name and which is an amount. Keep the two columns up for the rest of the lesson.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column is this digit standing in? Second rung, the phase's: how much is one piece of that column worth? Third rung: the chart is cut to the dot and the tenths column and the child fills both slots about the one digit in it. The name tray and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: the two phrases are one word apart, and the chapter's own worked example asks for place values and then begins every one of its five answer lines with the words the place of, so the page itself reads as though the two questions had one answer.
wrong.move: answers a place value question with the word tenths, which names the column again and never says how much.
wrong.screen: the word the child gave stays exactly where it was dropped and the slot headed place lights, because that is the slot it belongs in. The lit column is read out twice over, once as the name written above it and once as the size of the piece it counts, with that piece drawn underneath at its real size, and the slot headed worth is left open beside the answer already given.

wrong.why: the digit is the only number in sight and it is what would be read out if the column were ignored, which is exactly what a digit on its own is.
wrong.move: writes the digit itself into the worth slot, so the six in a number is said to be worth six.
wrong.screen: the digit is carried down out of its column into the rebuild bar as the bare number the child wrote, and the row is added with it: the total lands nowhere near the number the chart started from and is left standing beside it with the first pair that parts ringed in amber. The column is then read again with its heading lit and the piece it counts drawn under it.

phases.screen: one digit lit in the chart with the place slot and the worth slot both empty
phases.soWhat: The place of a digit is where it sits and is a name; the place value is what it is worth there and is an amount.
phases.concept: Place and place value are not the same word

phases.win: the total settles beside the number the chart started from and the two read the same
phases.does: carries every worth down into the bar, adds them, and reads the total
phases.goal: the place values of every digit add back to the number they came from
phases.says: Add all the worths together. Where should they land?
phases.check: Write the place value of every digit of a number of your own, add them all up, and say what the total should be.
phases.feels: the worths add back to the number they came out of, exactly, with nothing left over
phases.hands: Write out the place value of every digit of a number in a column down the page, then add the column up and see where it lands. Use that adding as the check on every place value question set for the rest of the week: a total that does not come back says a digit was given the wrong column, and it says so without anybody marking anything. Finish with the digit card game, agreeing first that the point card may not stand at either end of the line.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is this digit worth in its own column? Second rung, the phase's: what should all the worths come to together? Third rung: the chart is cut to two columns and the child gives both worths and adds them. The number pad and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: the digits are the numbers printed on the stage and adding them is the quickest thing that can be done with a row of numbers.
wrong.move: adds the digits themselves instead of what each one is worth in its own column.
wrong.screen: the bare digits come down into the rebuild bar exactly as the child sent them, the row adds itself and the small total stands beside the number the chart started from with the two read digit for digit and the first pair that parts ringed. The worths are then carried down into a second row underneath, added the same way, and both rows are left standing together.

wrong.why: the whole number part is where the large numbers are, and pieces smaller than one look like something that could not change a total much either way.
wrong.move: leaves the digits after the point out of the sum, because they are too small to make a difference.
wrong.screen: the worths of the whole number part alone are added in the bar and the total stands beside the number the chart started from, where it lands on a whole number and the reading parts at the dot column, which is left ringed. The three worths that were left out are then walked down into the row one at a time, each one changing the total as it lands, and the row is added again with the child's first total still standing above it.

phases.screen: every digit given its worth, with the rebuild bar empty along the foot
phases.soWhat: The place values of all the digits add back to the number they came from, and that is the check on every one of them.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the rebuild bar is added. The worths come down out of the chart one at a time along drawn paths, each one leaving its column lit behind it, and settle into the row in the order their columns stand in. The row adds itself from the right with the plus signs drawn between, and the total lifts across and stands beside a copy of the number the chart started from, where the two are read digit for digit from the left with each pair lighting as it is read. Move one digit into the wrong column and run it again: the row is built the same way, the total lands somewhere else, and the first pair that parts is left ringed in amber with nothing else marked.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the familiar chart stands ending at the ones column with plain ruled ground to its right and no headings on it. On the second a number is already dropped into the full chart with the headings turned face down, so the columns are there and unnamed. On the third one digit in the chart is lit and the two answer slots under it stand empty, one headed place and one headed worth. On the fourth every digit has been given its worth and the rebuild bar lies empty along the foot with its plus signs already drawn. The running count at the top left holds the digits settled against the digits the chart is holding, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the empty ground past the ones, or the face down heading over the lit digit, or the slot headed place, or the first worth waiting to come down, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what could come after the ones. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number in the chart, either slot, with the rebuild bar, the whole number bay and the card lane all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the columns past the ones, on counting places from the point, on the place against the place value, and on rebuilding a number from its worths.
voiceLines: Your chart stops at the ones. There is more of it than that.
Your chart stops at the ones. What could come after it?
Count along from the dot. Where does this one sit?
Where does it sit? Now say how much it is worth sitting there.
Add all the worths together. Where should they land?
Another number into the chart. One digit to a column.
Free play. Any number in the chart, both slots, rebuild bar and card lane open.
Count the columns again from the dot, and answer the two slots in order.
Every digit given a name and an amount, and every amount added back to where it came from.

observations.why: Each column is a tenth of the column on its left, and that rule does not run out at the ones.
observations.soWhat: The tenths, hundredths and thousandths places are the same chart continued, not a second chart.
observations.observe: The chart did not stop at the ones; it carried on rightwards through a column kept for the dot.

observations.why: The dot is the only mark in the number whose position does not depend on how many digits there are.
observations.soWhat: Count the decimal places from the point outwards, which is from the right of the point and not from the left of the number.
observations.observe: The counting of places always began at the dot, never at either end of the number.

observations.why: One of the two questions asks where a digit sits and the other asks how much it is worth sitting there.
observations.soWhat: The place is a name and the place value is an amount, and answering one with the other answers nothing.
observations.observe: The slot headed worth would not take the word tenths, and the slot headed place would not take an amount.

observations.why: Every digit's worth is exactly what that digit contributes, so together they are the whole number again.
observations.soWhat: Adding the worths is a check anyone can run, and a total that does not come back names a digit in the wrong column.
observations.observe: The worths added back to the number the chart started from, digit for digit.

source_tool.description: A place value chart fills the stage. The familiar columns stand on the left, thousands down to ones, and the chart then carries on past them: a narrow column holding the dot, and after it tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Digits are dropped in one to a column and a column already holding one refuses a second. Under the chart stand two answer slots side by side, one headed place and one headed worth, and neither will take the other's answer: a column name dropped into the worth slot springs back with the column it names lit and the slot still empty, and an amount dropped into the place slot springs back the same way. A rebuild bar runs along the foot of the stage. Every worth that has been given is carried down into it and added in a visible row, and the total is stood beside the number the chart started from, so a digit put in the wrong column shows up as a total that does not come back. A whole number bay to the left of the chart asks how many tens, hundreds or thousands sit inside a long whole number, which is this same chart read the other way. A card lane hands out digit cards and a single point card, and refuses an arrangement with the point standing first or last.
source_tool.art_direction: A ruled chart with a dot column / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip that can be cut, a ten by ten grid whose cells can be tapped, digit cards that can be picked up, a point card of its own, a ruled place chart with a heading over every column, a kitchen scale with a printing display, and a balance beam.

A whole is always drawn split into parts of the same size, with the parts touching so that the whole is still one thing. Exactly the stated number of parts is drawn, exactly the stated number of them is shaded, and no part overlaps another.

A decimal is always drawn with its point standing clearly between the two parts and never floating above or below the line. Where the two parts are named, the whole number part is named on the left and the decimal part on the right.

A place chart always carries a named heading over every column, holds one digit to a column, and keeps a column of its own for the dot between the ones and the tenths. A bare row of digits with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.

A zero filling an empty decimal place is drawn arriving from the point outwards, on the left of the digits already there, with a short arrow running inward from the point. That arrow never runs the other way.

A zero printed on the end of a decimal is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, and it is never dimmed, shrunk, tidied away or quietly dropped. The whole teaching of the closing topic is that it counts.

Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one above the other, with whatever measures the difference between them drawn in between. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A column, a place or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a part or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. A digit to the left of the point is deep blue and a digit to the right of it is green, with the decimal point itself vermilion between them in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose and one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and those three hold from the strip to the grid to the chart. A zero holding a place open is grey, whether it was filled in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement, because it is the one digit here doing a job rather than counting something. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. All of that holds in greyscale, because a filling zero is told apart by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a printed zero on the end by the place counter that lights it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the columns again from the dot, and answer the two slots in order.
voice.onNext: Another number into the chart. One digit to a column.
voice.opening: Your chart stops at the ones. There is more of it than that.
voice.onFinish: Every digit given a name and an amount, and every amount added back to where it came from.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number in the chart, both slots, rebuild bar and card lane open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The chart carries on past the point
Place and place value are not the same word

placement.where: After the chart has been drawn out by hand with the dot given a column of its own, and before any digit has been given a worth. The tool is what refuses to take a name where an amount was asked for, which a written answer on paper cannot refuse.

answer_key.rule: The place value chart carries on to the right of the ones place, past a dot, as tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and those three are the decimal places. The first digit after the point sits in the tenths place, the second in the hundredths and the third in the thousandths, and position alone decides it. The PLACE of a digit is where it sits, and it is a name, such as the tenths place. The PLACE VALUE of a digit is what it is worth there, and it is an amount, such as 5/10. Adding every digit's place value together rebuilds the number, and a total that does not come back means some digit was given the wrong column.
answer_key.wrong: The digit is lifted out and dropped back in with the columns counted aloud from the dot, and then the two slots are asked for again in order, the place first and the worth second. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The digits to the left of the point fill the familiar columns: 2 in the hundreds, 4 in the tens and 8 in the ones.
The dot takes a column of its own, straight after the ones.
The columns then carry on rightwards, so 5 goes in the tenths, 7 in the hundredths and 3 in the thousandths.
items.answer: 2 hundreds, 4 tens, 8 ones, then the dot, then 5 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths
items.question: Put 248.573 into a place value chart, one digit to a column, and name every column.
items.checkpoint: The decimal places run tenths, hundredths and thousandths to the right of the point.
items.misconception: Reading the columns after the point leftwards, the way the whole number columns are read.

steps: Count rightwards from the point: the first digit after it is in the tenths place, so the 4 is a tenth.
The second digit after the point is in the hundredths place, so the 8 sits there.
The third is in the thousandths place, so the 2 sits there. Position decides it, not the size of the digit.
items.answer: The 8 is in the hundredths place and the 2 is in the thousandths place
items.question: In 6.482, which place is the 8 in, and which place is the 2 in?
items.checkpoint: Position alone decides a digit's place, whatever the digit happens to be.
items.misconception: Giving the larger digit the larger place, so the 8 is put ahead of the 4.

steps: The 1 is the first digit to the right of the point, so its place is the tenths place, and that is a name.
Its place value is what the digit is worth sitting in that column, which is one tenth.
So the place is tenths and the place value is 1/10, or 0.1. One of those is a name and the other is an amount.
items.answer: Its place is the tenths place, and its place value is 1/10, which is 0.1
items.question: In 34.16, give the place of the 1, and then give its place value.
items.checkpoint: The place says where a digit sits; the place value says how much it is worth there.
items.misconception: Answering a place value question with the word tenths, which names the column again and never says how much.

steps: The 2 sits in the tens place, so its place value is 20, and the 3 sits in the ones, so its place value is 3.
After the point, the 4 is worth 4/10, the 5 is worth 5/100 and the 1 is worth 1/1000.
Adding all five worths gives 23.451 back exactly, which is the check that every digit was given the right column.
items.question: Write the place value of every digit of 23.451, and add them all together.
items.checkpoint: The place values of all the digits add back to the number they came from.
items.misconception: Adding the digits themselves instead of what each one is worth in its own column.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many tens are there in 5,470?
Which three places come after the point on the chart, and in what order?
In 7.328, which place is the 3 in?
How many hundreds are there in 48,600?
In 91.507, give the place of the 7, and then give its place value.
items.final_answer: Its place is the thousandths place, and its place value is 7/1000, which is 0.007

items.question: A child is asked for the place value of the 6 in 5.63 and answers tenths. What is wrong with that answer?
items.final_answer: Tenths is the name of the place, not the worth; the place value is 6/10, which is 0.6

items.question: Write the place value of every digit of 52.874, and add them all up.
Six digit cards and one point card are held up and make 472.836. Add the place values of all six digits and say what they come to.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: puts one digit in one column and refuses a second digit in the same column
extends the columns past the ones, through the dot, to tenths, hundredths and thousandths
counts the columns rightwards from the dot and names each one
takes the name of the column a digit sits in
takes the amount that digit is worth there, and refuses a name
adds every worth given and stands the total beside the number the chart started from
asks how many tens, hundreds or thousands sit inside a long whole number
hands out digit cards and one point card, and will not let the point stand first or last

teaching_notes: Draw the chart by hand first, with the dot given a column of its own, and write every heading in before a single digit goes anywhere. The chapter's own worked example drops 367.912 into the chart a digit at a time, and that one is worth doing together before the tool is opened. Then take the two words apart and keep them apart. Ask for the place first and the worth second, in that order, every single time, and never accept one for the other. A class reading the chapter cold will learn them as one word, because the worked example that goes through 12.563 digit by digit asks for place values and then answers every one of its five lines with the word place. The five worths themselves are right: ten, two, five tenths, six hundredths and three thousandths, and they add back to 12.563 exactly. Use that adding as the check on every place value question you set. A total that does not rebuild the number says a digit was given the wrong column, and it says so without anybody having to mark anything. The digit card lab at the end of the chapter is this whole topic standing up. Put the point card in the middle before the holders arrange themselves. As printed, they stand in any order, and a point at either end builds something the chapter has not taught and the step after it cannot be answered about.
generation_prompt: Build a place value chart tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. The chart fills the working area with a named heading over every column: thousands, hundreds, tens and ones on the left, then a narrow column holding the dot, then tenths, hundredths and thousandths. A grow control extends the chart past the ones and names each new column as it appears. Digits are dragged in one to a column, and a column already holding a digit refuses a second one and springs it back. A count control runs rightwards from the dot, lighting and naming each column in turn. Under the chart sit two answer slots side by side, one headed place and one headed worth. The place slot takes only a column name and the worth slot takes only an amount, and either one handed the other's answer springs it back with the column it names lit and the slot left empty, nothing marked. A rebuild bar along the foot of the stage collects every worth that has been given, adds them in a visible row, and stands the total beside the number the chart started from. A whole number bay to the left of the chart takes a long whole number and asks how many tens, hundreds or thousands sit inside it. A card lane hands out digit cards and a single point card for holders to arrange, and refuses an arrangement with the point first or last, saying which rule it broke. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put one digit in each column. Count the columns from the dot to find a place. Write the name of the place in the first slot. Write what the digit is worth in the second slot. Add all the worths up to check.
